summary: Describes heuristics that help Telnet implementations of the Environment option work with others, by identifying which definitions of VAR and VALUE the other side is using.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet implementations disagreed about the meanings of VAR and VALUE in the Environment option. RFC 1571 gives clients and servers clues for detecting the peer's convention, and says to assume the peer is correct when those clues do not decide the issue.

questions: what is the telnet environment option
why are var and value reversed in telnet
how to detect reversed var and value in telnet
subtitle: Rules of thumb for Telnet peers that disagree about the meanings of VAR and VALUE.

tldr.problem: RFC 1408 defines Telnet Environment option values VAR and VALUE in the reverse order from the BSD implementation, so implementations may interpret exchanged data differently.
tldr.mechanism: Clients inspect SEND suboptions, while servers inspect IS or INFO suboptions, and use clues in the contents to infer which definitions the peer uses.
tldr.outcome: The heuristics can help implementations work with either convention. When the evidence is inconclusive, the memo says to assume the peer uses the correct definitions.

facts.label: Default when tests are inconclusive
facts.value: Assume the peer uses the correct definitions

today: RFC 1571 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1408. The unit metadata records no later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why VAR and VALUE Were Confusing
sections.content:
RFC 1408 defines VAR and VALUE in the reverse order from the BSD implementation of the Telnet Environment option. The BSD implementation was the reference implementation that RFC 1408 was intended to document, and the RFC says it formed the basis for many existing implementations. This difference created an interoperability problem.

RFC 1571 updates RFC 1408 with heuristics, or practical tests, for identifying which definitions the other side uses. These tests help an implementation decide how to parse and generate Environment option suboptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The written specification and the BSD implementation gave two labels opposite meanings. This memo gives programs tests for detecting which version the other side follows.

sections.title: How a Client Checks a SEND Suboption
sections.content:
A Telnet client checks a SEND suboption from the server. The suboption should contain VAR and USERVAR, not VALUE. If the client finds VALUE, it should assume the server has reversed the definitions and reverse its own interpretation when parsing the rest of the suboption and generating IS or INFO.

If both VALUE and VAR appear, the SEND suboption is malformed and the result depends on the implementation. If neither appears, the client cannot tell which convention the server uses and should assume the server has the correct definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: A client expects a SEND suboption not to contain VALUE. If VALUE appears, the client treats the server's definitions as reversed; if there is no clue, it assumes they are correct.

sections.title: How a Server Checks IS and INFO
sections.content:
A Telnet server examines the client's IS or INFO suboption. If the marker is followed by VAR, the client is assumed to use the correct definitions; if it is followed by VALUE, the definitions are assumed to be reversed. If it is followed by USERVAR, the server applies further tests because either VAR or VALUE may legally follow a USERVAR.

The tests look for consecutive markers or empty values, then compare counts of VAR, USERVAR, and VALUE, and then check whether variable names appear in VAR or VALUE contents. The memo's summary gives the decision for each pattern. If the tests do not settle the issue, the server assumes the client uses the correct definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: A server checks the client's IS or INFO suboption for patterns that reveal which labels it uses. It checks simple markers first, then counts and familiar variable names; if no test decides, it assumes the client's definitions are correct.

references.text: Borman, D., Editor, "Telnet Environment Option", RFC 1408, Cray Research, Inc., January 1993.
